exercises.title: The slow duplicate check
exercises.task: Read HasDuplicateSlow, then press Run. It runs the function on 2 000 to 16 000 values with no duplicate (the worst case: every pair is compared) and prints the comparisons and the time. Look at both ratio columns. Run it twice: the comparisons never change; the time wobbles, a lot when n is small. That difference is why Big O counts steps, not seconds.

exercises.title: The fast duplicate check
exercises.task: Fill the two holes so HasDuplicate uses the map. Run compares it with the slow version; Check tests it, including on 300 000 values.
hints: A map answers "have I seen this value?" in one step, whatever its size.
In Go, seen[x] is false for a key that was never set.
Hole 1: if seen[x] { return true }. Hole 2 is one assignment.

exercises.title: Read the growth
exercises.task: Four functions count the steps they take for a given n. Before running anything, read each one and write its growth in Answers. Then Run: it doubles n and prints the ratio, so you can check yourself. Check grades the answers.
hints: Ask for each loop: when n doubles, how many more times does it run?
A loop that halves its counter each time runs about log₂(n) times. A loop with a fixed upper bound does not grow at all.
Two of the four look like something they are not: one is nested but grows linearly, one has a loop but stops growing.
